vignette:
Eleanor first came to my office on a crisp autumn afternoon, smelling faintly of pine needles and damp earth. At 73, she has the sturdy, weathered look of the trees she has spent her life tending. For over forty years, she worked as a forester, a job she speaks of with a quiet, steady reverence. The forest, she explained, has rules. A tree grows towards the light. Its rings tell a true story. It is predictable, logical. It was, for most of her life, the only place she ever felt safe.

Her story begins not in the expansive quiet of the woods, but in the suffocating silence of a small post-war kitchen. She was the only child of a widowed mother, a woman who Eleanor describes with a detached precision, as if cataloging a species of blighted tree. Her mother’s moods were governed by the level of gin in the bottle on the counter. When the bottle was full, the house was tense with a coiled silence. As it emptied, the silence would break. A spilled glass of milk, a scuff mark on the floor, a question asked at the wrong moment—any of it could be the spark.

Eleanor learned early to make herself small, to read the atmospheric pressure of the house. She remembers the specific sound of her mother’s footsteps on the linoleum, a heavy, rhythmic tread that meant a storm was coming. The abuse was methodical, delivered with a wooden spoon or a belt, and always followed by the same chilling pronouncement: “This is to make you good.” Eleanor would retreat inward, focusing on the grain of the wooden spoon, the cracks in the linoleum, the dust motes dancing in the sliver of light under the door. She learned to dissociate from her body, to become an observer of her own pain. She believed, with the unshakeable faith of a child, that she was fundamentally bad, and that the pain was her due.

She left home at seventeen and never looked back. The forest service was a refuge. The solitude was a balm. Out in the vast wilderness, there were no sudden footsteps, no unpredictable rages. The only sounds were the wind in the pines and the crack of a branch underfoot. She learned the land, acre by acre, until it was more familiar to her than any human face. She married once, a kind man from the parks department, but the intimacy felt like a cage. She couldn’t sleep with another person’s weight in the bed, couldn’t bear to be touched without warning. She’d flinch if he came up behind her too quietly. She knew he deserved more than the sliver of herself she could offer, and the marriage ended after a few years of pained, polite distance. She chalked it up to her being, as she puts it, “poor soil for that sort of thing.”

For decades, she managed. The past was a locked room, and she had no intention of finding the key. But three months ago, her mother died. Eleanor went to the funeral out of a sense of duty, standing stiffly by the grave, feeling nothing. She expected relief, a final closing of a chapter. Instead, the door to that locked room blew off its hinges.

Now, the smell of gin will rise up out of nowhere when she’s inventorying a stand of firs. The image of her mother’s face, tight with fury, flashes in her mind as she’s trying to fall asleep. She wakes up gasping, the phantom sensation of cold linoleum on her cheek. The familiar sounds of the forest have turned menacing; a snapping twig sends a jolt of pure terror through her, her heart hammering as if the heavy footsteps have finally caught up. The woods, her lifelong sanctuary, now feel fraught with ambush. She looks at her own hands, gnarled with age and hard work, and sees the small, trembling hands of a child who believes she is wicked and is only waiting for the punishment to begin.
